bodyHtml:
A TMT bar quotation should tell you exactly what will arrive at your construction site. The grade, sizes, quantity and delivery terms all deserve attention before you agree to a price.

The main factors to consider when buying TMT bars are the structural specification, BIS certification, test documentation, corrosion exposure, dimensions, supplier reliability and total delivered cost.

Working through these details helps you compare suppliers fairly and identify discrepancies before the steel is used.

1 Choose the grade specified in your structural drawings

Start with the material specification prepared by your structural engineer. It should identify the required steel grade and reinforcement details.

The number in a grade such as Fe 500 or Fe 550 indicates the specified minimum yield or proof stress. The D suffix identifies a category with enhanced minimum elongation requirements compared with the corresponding grade without D. BIS grade definitions (PDF)

Write the complete designation on your purchase order. Fe 550 and Fe 550D should not be treated as identical specifications.

If a supplier proposes a different grade, have the change reviewed before ordering. A higher strength number does not automatically make the replacement suitable, and it does not authorise a reduction in bar quantity.

2 Verify BIS certification and the licence details

For TMT reinforcement supplied to IS 1786, ask for the manufacturer’s BIS certification details and CM/L licence number.

Use the Verify Licence Details feature in the BIS Care app to check the licence. Confirm the manufacturer and manufacturing location, current status, applicable standard and product coverage. BIS Care verification guidance

The licence scope should cover the relevant grade and size. A brand name or an ISI logo printed on a brochure is insufficient evidence on its own.

This check is particularly useful when purchasing through a new supplier or receiving material from a different manufacturing unit.

3 Ask for a mill test certificate that matches the delivery

A mill test certificate, or MTC, records the test results associated with the supplied steel.

BIS requires each consignment of BIS-certified material to have a certificate identifying the cast or lot, grade, size and corresponding results. Match those details with the bundle identification and delivery documents. BIS product manuals (search IS 1786)

Agree on document availability before payment and dispatch. A sample report from the manufacturer may demonstrate the report format, but it does not establish the properties of a different batch.

Keep the MTC with the invoice and delivery record so the material remains traceable after unloading.

4 Review strength ductility and bending performance together

The grade label is a starting point. The test results show how the material performed.

Ask your project engineer to review yield or proof stress, tensile strength and elongation against the specification. Where required, the tensile-to-yield ratio and total elongation at maximum force also need attention.

Bend and rebend results provide additional information about behaviour under prescribed bending conditions. These checks complement tensile testing. Reinforcing steel test parameters

Avoid judging the steel through a single number or an informal bending demonstration. The complete set of required properties matters.

5 Consider corrosion exposure at the project site

Tell your engineer and supplier about the environment in which the reinforcement will be used. Coastal exposure, saline groundwater and aggressive industrial conditions may require additional durability measures.

Corrosion resistance is a separate consideration from strength grade. A higher Fe number does not establish better protection against corrosion.

ARS, for example, offers both Fe 550D and CRS Fe 550D products. Its CRS variant is intended for applications requiring enhanced corrosion resistance. Review the ARS product comparison against your project requirements.

Ask for supporting test information when comparing corrosion-resistant products. Concrete quality, adequate cover and construction practices also remain part of the durability strategy.

6 Check bar sizes lengths and weight

Your order should specify the nominal diameter, required length and quantity for each item.

At delivery, arrange for representative lengths and their weight to be checked against the applicable IS 1786 requirements for the ordered size. The standard treats nominal size, effective cross-sectional area, mass and surface characteristics as distinct checks. BIS product manuals (search IS 1786)

Because TMT bars have raised ribs, a measurement across the outermost ribs alone is not a reliable confirmation of nominal diameter.

Also clarify the commercial weighing basis. Ask how the delivered weight will be established and recorded, particularly when comparing quotations expressed per kilogram, tonne, piece or bundle.

7 Inspect surface condition and handling damage

Inspect the delivered bars for visible cracks, deep pitting, heavy scaling, damaged ribs and contamination such as oil or grease.

Rust needs a measured assessment. A thin layer of firmly attached surface rust is different from corrosion that causes material loss. The Concrete Reinforcing Steel Institute advises checking whether rust has reduced bar weight, cross-sectional area or rib dimensions below applicable requirements. CRSI guidance on reinforcement condition

Refer significant corrosion or damage to the project engineer before acceptance or use. The material must still satisfy the applicable requirements.

For related inspection points, read how to check TMT bar quality before buying.

8 Choose a supplier whose identity and service you can verify

Check the supplier’s business details and confirm any claim of authorised dealership with the manufacturer.

A dependable supplier should explain where the material comes from, provide a clear invoice and arrange the required quality documents. Ask who will handle shortages, damaged material or a mismatch between the order and delivery.

Discuss availability across the full range of sizes you need. A competitive quotation has limited value if a missing diameter holds up reinforcement work.

Get the terms for returns, replacements and order changes in writing. This is especially useful when purchases are split across several construction stages.

9 Compare the total delivered cost

Compare quotations for the same manufacturer, grade, product variant, size mix and quantity.

Then check what each price includes.

Quotation itemWhat to confirm
Material ratePrice unit and the exact product covered
Quantity basisActual weighed mass, calculated mass or another agreed basis
TaxesIncluded in the quotation or charged separately
TransportDelivery charge to your specific site
Loading and unloadingResponsibility, equipment and additional charges
ProcessingCost of any requested cutting or bending
Validity and paymentHow long the rate applies and when payment is due
DeliveryDispatch commitment and arrangements for partial supplies

These details can explain why two apparently similar rates produce different final bills.

Use an approved reinforcement schedule for purchase quantities. Estimates based on floor area can support early budgeting, but the final order should reflect the design and construction plan.

10 Plan delivery storage and material identification

Before placing the order, confirm that the site can receive and store the steel.

Check vehicle access, unloading arrangements and the sequence in which different sizes will be needed. Buying the entire requirement at once may be inconvenient where space is limited or construction will continue over several months.

Store bars on suitable supports, clear of soil and standing water. Keep grades and sizes organised, and preserve bundle identification so the material can be linked to its documents.

Industry guidance on reinforcement handling recommends checking incoming material against shipping information and organising it for the intended work sequence. CRSI handling and storage guidance

For staged deliveries, agree on quantities, dates and how future prices will be determined.

What to confirm when the delivery arrives

Have the purchase order, delivery note and relevant test documents available during receipt.

Check that the manufacturer, grade and size mix match the order. Record the quantity received, inspect the material’s condition and retain the identification needed for traceability.

Photograph and document any discrepancy before bundles are mixed with existing stock. Resolve concerns with the supplier and project team before the affected material enters fabrication.

Frequently asked questions about buying TMT bars

Which TMT bar grade is best for house construction

Use the grade specified by the structural engineer. The appropriate choice depends on the design, loads, detailing and site conditions. A recommendation based only on the number of floors is incomplete.

How can I check whether TMT bars are genuine

Verify the manufacturer’s BIS licence details, inspect product and bundle identification, and match the delivery with its MTC and invoice. Confirm the supplier’s relationship with the manufacturer where an authorised dealership is claimed.

Does a colour change mean TMT bars should be rejected

Surface discolouration alone does not determine whether TMT bars are suitable for use. Check for loose rust, heavy scaling, pitting or visible loss of steel section. Ask the project engineer to assess suspected corrosion and confirm compliance with project specifications before acceptance.

Is it better to buy TMT bars in bulk

That depends on your project size, storage capacity, cash flow and supplier terms. Compare bulk and staged-delivery quotations, including transport and handling. A bulk discount is useful only when the material can be stored and managed appropriately.

Prepare a clear enquiry before you buy

A useful enquiry includes the specified grade, product variant, bar sizes, quantities, site location and required delivery dates. Ask the supplier to confirm the supporting documents and total delivered price.
